Sector momentum - top 3 of 9 SPDR sectors, monthly rebalance

Statistical validation and engine analysis   5032 observations · 252 periods per year

Is the measured edge real, and is the backtest that measured it trustworthy?

Falsified

This tool falsifies; it cannot validate. It finds reasons to disbelieve a backtest, never reasons to believe one. The findings below are what the tests actually established. Nothing here says the strategy cannot work - only that this backtest does not show that it does.

Findings (1)

Critical Returns are explained by factor exposure ATTR-LEVERED-BETA

The returns are explained by exposures you can buy directly: alpha is -1.03% a year with a t-statistic of -0.70 (p=0.484) and the factors explain 85% of the variance; correlation to SPY is 0.89 and the strategy adds -0.020 annualised Sharpe over simply holding it at 0.99x leverage.

What to do: Hedge the factor exposures and re-test the residual, which is the only part that could be alpha.

What could not be tested

  • Matched-exposure random-entry test: the position series is multi-asset. This test asks whether a single instrument was timed well, and reordering a cross-sectional book in time does not answer that question.

Headline

Every Sharpe ratio on this page is annualised to 252 periods unless the row says otherwise. Every one of them is also computed on returns in excess of the risk-free rate (1.56% a year over this sample), and the benchmark is treated identically. Total return, drawdown and Calmar are left on total returns, because those describe the path an investor lived through.

The book is on average 94% invested. If the backtest did not credit the idle balance at the bill rate, the return series understates by about 0.09% a year - in the opposite direction to the adjustment above, and worth checking before reading the excess figures as final.

MeasureValue95% interval
Annualised Sharpe (naive annualisation) 0.51 0.11 to 0.91
Autocorrelation-adjusted (Lo 2002) 0.57 0.12 to 1.01
Per-period Sharpe0.0321 0.0070 to 0.0573

The interval is a stationary bootstrap with a Politis-White block length of 6.2 over 2000 resamples - not the analytic standard error, which assumes away the serial dependence these returns have.

Lo's adjustment moves the annualisation factor from 15.87 to 17.63, raising the annualised Sharpe by 11.0%: these returns are negatively autocorrelated at short lags, so naive sqrt(q) annualisation was too harsh.

Caveat: annualising to 252 periods implies a sum over 251 lags, but 5032 observations can only speak to about 76; the adjustment assumes no dependence beyond that, and cannot rule out longer-horizon persistence.

Attribution: is the edge just factor exposure?

Regression of excess strategy returns on the Fama-French factors. Alpha is the intercept - what is left once the factors are accounted for. A p-value above 0.05 means the strategy has not been shown to add anything the factors do not already explain.

R-squared 84.9% over 5032 observations. Standard errors: Newey-West HAC, 76 lags. Regression residuals from a return series are serially correlated, and plain OLS standard errors would understate the uncertainty on alpha - the one coefficient the whole exercise turns on.

How much of this was the path it took?

Maximum drawdown is an extreme-value statistic, and one realisation of it says much less than it appears to. These are the same returns resampled in blocks, so the distributions show how different the headline figures could plausibly have been on another draw of the same process.

StatisticRealised Resampled median5th to 95th percentile Realised percentile
Total return 550.80% 566.11% 81.78% to 2140.50% 49%
Annualised Sharpe 0.51 0.52 0.17 to 0.86 49%
Maximum drawdown -48.00% -39.13% -58.29% to -26.46% 19%
Drawdown a matched random walk would expect -40.82% same drift and volatility IID normal, no fat tails 25%

Both comparisons understate, and in opposite ways. block resampling with a mean block of 6.2 periods cannot reassemble drawdowns that unfolded over much longer horizons, so the resampled distribution understates how deep a drawdown this strategy can produce. The matched random walk assumes IID normal returns, so it has neither volatility clustering nor fat tails and will also come out shallower than reality. A realised drawdown far outside both means the loss came from the order in which returns arrived, and neither baseline can recreate it.

Selection bias

BHY-adjusted t-statistic 2.27 → 1.37
t-statistic BHY needs at 24 trials 2.72 · annualised Sharpe 0.68
Rank of this result among the trials 12 of 24 by t-statistic

Deflation runs on returns net of 3 bps, the upper end of realistic cost for US large-cap ETFs, so this figure sits slightly below the gross Sharpe in the headline. Trial-Sharpe dispersion measured from 24 trial columns. Sharpe ratios in this table are per-period because that is the scale the Deflated Sharpe is defined on; scaling both sides would not change the comparison.

The two selection tests here answer different questions and can disagree. The Deflated Sharpe asks whether this result beats the best of 24 draws from a no-edge null; the Harvey-Liu BHY haircut asks whether the t-statistic survives a false-discovery correction across 24 tests. They disagree on this sample: the Deflated Sharpe clears its bar at 0.969 while BHY takes the t-statistic to 1.37 (p = 0.169), which is not significant. Read the selection-bias conclusion as unsettled rather than passed: one of the two standard corrections does not clear it.

The trial count prices the configurations declared for this backtest. An effect taken from published work arrives with a search history of its own - the papers that found it, and the ones that were never written - and nothing in this report can see that. Read 24 as a floor on the number of things that were tried, not as the number of things that were tried.

Simulated null: the observed result sits at the 99.0% percentile of 1500 replications (p = 0.011). Validity check: the simulation and the closed form disagree by 32.1% - trial Sharpes have fatter tails than the normal approximation assumes, so the analytic Deflated Sharpe under-penalises and the real bar is higher.

The degradation slope is deliberately not reported as evidence, and neither is the in-sample-against-out-of-sample scatter that usually accompanies this chart. CSCV splits one fixed sample into complementary halves, so the two Sharpes sum to a constant: the scatter falls on a line of slope near -1 whatever the strategy does, and the apparent decay is an identity rather than a finding. The right-hand panel shows what the winner actually earns out of sample instead.

Robustness

TestResultReading
Annualised Sharpe, low / high volatility 0.74 / 0.44 same sign
Annualised Sharpe across 20 start dates 0.51 to 0.82 stable
Profit concentration vs a normal baseline 1.43x as expected
Annualised Sharpe dropping the best 1% / 5% of periods -0.11 / -1.50 from 0.51
Sign-flip randomisation p-value 0.006 signal informative
Parameter neighbourhood retention 97.4% plateau

The post-drop Sharpe falls steeply for almost any strategy - removing the best 5% of periods from a Sharpe-0.51 series is expected to push it below zero, which is why the concentration ratio, not the post-drop Sharpe, is what this test actually reads. A ratio near 1.0 means the profit is no more concentrated than the Sharpe alone implies.

Engine analysis: can this backtest be trusted as an implementation?

Independent of whether the strategy makes money. A sound-looking number from an unsound implementation is the more dangerous of the two failures, because nothing in the return series betrays it.

CheckResultDetail
Reads the future? no none beyond 22 periods
Same input, same output? yes 3 calls compared
Is there a decision to examine? yes 126 changes over 5032 periods, 5.8% of it flat
Survives being traded a period late? 96.8% retained Sharpe 0.51 to 0.49 annualised
Universe complete over the sample? yes all 9 instruments

No dependence on data more than about 22 periods after the decision point. The strategy revises its position every 22 periods on average, and a leak shorter than that is overwritten before it reaches the book.

Trading cost and trading delay are different questions and fail independently. A monthly rotation across liquid funds can absorb hundreds of basis points in fees and still lose its entire edge to a single session of delay, because the signal was picking up a reversal that had already reverted by the time anyone could act on it.

A universe of survivors looks exactly like a universe, so survivorship cannot be read out of the returns - it has to be declared, or counted against a point-in-time membership list. Inclusion timing is the part that is visible in the price data on its own: an instrument added the day it listed was chosen in the knowledge that it would exist.

Universe: declared point-in-time - it was not assembled from present-day membership, so nothing entered it with hindsight. Declared, not measured. All nine original SPDR sector funds have traded continuously since 1998, so the universe is fixed for the whole sample and there is no survivorship question. XLRE and XLC are deliberately excluded because they launched mid-sample, and adding an instrument the day it lists is a subtle way to buy hindsight.
